title: FAR U5·W2 — Current Liabilities, Contingencies & Commitments
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the obligations side

The current-liabilities section reports what MBG owes within the year — payables, accruals, warranty reserves — plus the harder judgments of contingencies and commitments. The recognition question is sharp: some obligations are recorded, some are only disclosed, and some are ignored entirely. This week works the classification of current liabilities, the ASC 450 contingency framework, and the related estimates (warranties, compensated absences, asset retirement obligations) that turn uncertain future outflows into today's liabilities.

Defining current liabilities

A current liability is an obligation expected to be settled within one year or the operating cycle, whichever is longer, using current assets or by creating another current liability. The category includes accounts payable, accrued liabilities (wages, interest, taxes payable), the current portion of long-term debt, and unearned revenue. A short-term obligation expected to be refinanced on a long-term basis is classified as noncurrent only if the entity both intends to refinance and has the ability (a noncancelable agreement) to do so — otherwise it stays current.

Accruals: payroll and compensated absences

Several liabilities accrue as employees work. Payroll liabilities include amounts withheld from employees (income tax, the employee share of FICA) and the employer's own payroll taxes (the matching FICA, unemployment) — the withheld amounts are a liability until remitted. Compensated absences (vacation, sick pay) are accrued when the right vests or accumulates, the obligation relates to services already rendered, payment is probable, and the amount is estimable — so MBG records a vacation liability as employees earn the time, not when they take it.

Warranties

A product or service warranty creates a liability for the estimated future cost of honoring it. An assurance-type warranty (the product will work as promised) is not a separate performance obligation — the entity accrues the estimated warranty cost as an expense in the period of sale (matching). A service-type warranty (an extended or separately priced warranty) is a separate performance obligation under ASC 606, so its price is deferred and recognized as revenue over the coverage period. Worked example: if MBG estimates warranty costs at 2% of $5,000,000 in sales, it accrues a $100,000 warranty expense and liability, drawing the liability down as actual repairs occur.

Loss contingencies — the ASC 450 framework

A loss contingency — pending litigation, a product recall, a guarantee — is evaluated on two axes: the likelihood of the loss and whether it is reasonably estimable. The rule: if a loss is probable AND estimable, accrue it (record the liability and expense; use the best estimate, or the low end of a range when no amount is better than another). If it is only reasonably possible (or probable but not estimable), disclose it in the notes. If it is remote, generally ignore it (with narrow exceptions, like guarantees). This probable/reasonably-possible/remote matrix is one of FAR's most tested judgments.

Gain contingencies and commitments

Gain contingencies are treated conservatively: they are not accrued (to avoid recognizing income before it is realized) and are disclosed only when their realization is probable. Commitments — such as a noncancelable purchase commitment to buy materials at a fixed price — are generally disclosed, but if the contracted price has fallen below market by year-end, the entity recognizes a loss on the purchase commitment for the decline, paralleling lower-of-cost rules. The asymmetry — accrue probable losses, defer gains — reflects accounting conservatism.

Asset retirement obligations

An asset retirement obligation (ARO) under ASC 410 is a legal obligation to retire a long-lived asset — to dismantle a structure or restore a site at the end of its use. The entity recognizes the ARO at the fair value (present value) of the future cost when incurred, with a corresponding increase to the asset's carrying amount; the asset portion is then depreciated and the liability is accreted (accretion expense) up to its future settlement amount. For a contractor with site-restoration duties, the ARO puts the eventual cleanup cost on the balance sheet the day the obligation arises.

Other current liabilities

Several recurring items round out the section. Unearned (deferred) revenue — a customer deposit or advance — is a liability until the performance obligation is satisfied. Premiums and coupons (customer-incentive programs) require accruing the estimated cost of redemptions outstanding. Refundable deposits and sales-tax payable (collected from customers and owed to the government) are liabilities, not revenue. Each reflects the same principle: an inflow the entity has not yet earned, or an amount it holds on behalf of others, is an obligation rather than income.

Accruing bonuses and other estimated costs

Many obligations require estimating an amount tied to results. A bonus or profit-sharing liability is accrued when the entity has a present obligation from past service and the amount is estimable — sometimes computed as a percentage of income, which can be circular when the bonus is based on income after the bonus, requiring an algebraic solution. Property taxes are accrued ratably over the fiscal period they cover. The common thread is the accrual principle: an expense and liability are recorded in the period the obligating event occurs, not when cash is eventually paid.

Contingencies in practice: litigation and guarantees

The contingency rules are applied most often to litigation. The entity, with counsel, assesses the likelihood of an unfavorable outcome and the range of loss; a letter of audit inquiry to the client's attorney (from AUD) corroborates the assessment. Guarantees are a special case — even a remote guarantee of another's debt is disclosed, and a standby guarantee is initially recognized at fair value as a liability. These applications show the matrix is not mechanical: it requires judgment about probability and estimability, exactly the area where management bias is a risk.

Exit and disposal costs

One more accrual deserves note: a liability for exit or disposal activities (restructuring) — such as one-time termination benefits or the cost to vacate a facility — is recognized only when the obligation is incurred, not when management merely commits to a plan. A liability cannot be booked simply because a restructuring was announced; there must be a present obligation meeting the recognition criteria. This rule prevents the old practice of front-loading a large "big bath" restructuring reserve, and it reinforces that a liability requires a genuine present obligation, not just an intention.

CMA bridge

The CMA program forecasts MBG's payables and accrued costs for the cash budget; FAR decides which obligations are recognized versus merely disclosed. The contingency matrix is exactly the judgment a CFO faces with a pending construction-defect claim — accrue, disclose, or ignore — and it directly affects reported liabilities and equity.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify current vs noncurrent (≤ 1 year/operating cycle); keep a refinanceable short-term obligation current unless intent AND ability to refinance exist.
  2. Accrue payroll withholdings, compensated absences (vesting/accumulating), and assurance-type warranties; defer service-type warranty revenue.
  3. Apply ASC 450: probable + estimable → accrue (low end of a range if needed); reasonably possible → disclose; remote → ignore. Gain contingencies are not accrued.
  4. Record an ARO at present value with accretion + depreciation; treat unearned revenue, premiums, deposits, and sales tax as liabilities.

Recap: current liabilities settle within a year or the operating cycle, and a refinanceable short-term debt stays current absent both intent and ability to refinance; entities accrue payroll, compensated absences, and assurance-type warranties (2% of $5,000,000 sales = a $100,000 accrual) while deferring service-type warranty revenue; ASC 450 accrues a loss that is probable and estimable, discloses a reasonably possible one, and ignores a remote one, with gain contingencies never accrued; and an ARO is recorded at present value with later accretion and depreciation.

flashcards.back: Settled within one year or the operating cycle (whichever is longer) using current assets or by creating another current liability.
Classify as noncurrent ONLY if the entity intends to refinance AND has the ability (noncancelable agreement); otherwise it stays current.
Assurance (works as promised): accrue estimated cost as expense at sale (not a separate obligation). Service-type (extended/priced): a separate ASC 606 obligation — defer revenue over coverage.
Probable AND estimable → ACCRUE (best estimate; low end of range if none better). Reasonably possible (or not estimable) → DISCLOSE. Remote → ignore.
Never accrued (conservatism); disclose only if realization is probable.
A noncancelable fixed-price purchase commitment whose market price falls below contract price by year-end → recognize a loss for the decline.
Recognize legal retirement obligation at fair value (PV) when incurred + add to asset cost; later depreciate the asset and accrete the liability (accretion expense).
Accrue when the right vests or accumulates, relates to services already rendered, payment is probable, and the amount is estimable.

questions.q: A loss contingency is accrued when it is:
questions.explain: ASC 450 requires accrual when a loss is both probable and reasonably estimable; reasonably possible losses are disclosed.

questions.q: When a loss is probable and the estimate is a range with no better point in it, the entity accrues:
choices: The low end of the range
questions.explain: If no amount in the range is a better estimate, the minimum (low end) is accrued.

choices: Not accrued; disclosed only if probable
questions.explain: Conservatism prevents accruing gain contingencies; disclose only if realization is probable.

questions.q: An assurance-type warranty is accounted for by:
choices: Accruing estimated warranty cost as expense in the period of sale
Deferring revenue over the coverage period
Recording it only when claims are paid
questions.explain: Assurance warranties accrue estimated cost at sale; service-type warranties defer revenue under ASC 606.

questions.q: Warranty estimated at 2% of $5,000,000 sales produces a warranty expense/liability of:
questions.explain: 2% × $5,000,000 = $100,000 accrued at the time of sale.

questions.q: A short-term obligation may be classified as noncurrent only if the entity:
choices: Intends and has the ability to refinance long-term
questions.explain: Both intent and demonstrated ability (e.g., a noncancelable refinancing agreement) are required.

questions.q: An asset retirement obligation is initially measured at:
choices: The present value (fair value) of the future retirement cost
questions.explain: An ARO is recognized at fair value (present value) when incurred, with later accretion to the settlement amount.
